probes.support_reason: PARTIAL under P-a (SUBSTITUTED WEAKER MECHANISM). This is the central Rust finding of chunk A and it is a language fact, not an authoring choice. Sub-requirements (1) and (3) are delivered in full: `let x = vec![1, 2, 3];` binds a local to Rust's normal growable integer sequence containing 1, 2, 3, and `x[0]` reads element 0 after the call and is produced as the result (the wrapper prints 1). Sub-requirement (2) is NOT delivered as written. It demands the plainest ordinary call-site syntax 'with NO extra sigil, address-of, borrow marker, copy, clone, wrapper, annotation, or modifier at the argument position'. In Rust a bare `f(x)` on a `Vec<i32>` MOVES the operand, because Reference 'Call expressions' passes arguments by value and `Vec<T>` is not `Copy`; the caller's binding is then dead and sub-requirement (3) cannot be delivered. Refutation witness witnesses/F05.P1/rust/REFUT_byvalue_bare_call: with `fn f(v: Vec<i32>) -> i32` and a byte-identical bare `f(x);`, rustc rejects the fragment with `error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `x` ... value borrowed here after move`. Conversely, declaring the parameter `&Vec<i32>` does not make the bare form legal, because Rust inserts no implicit borrow at an argument position: refutation witness witnesses/F05.P1/rust/REFUT_bare_call_ref_param gives `error[E0308]: mismatched types: expected `&Vec<i32>`, found `Vec<{integer}>`` with the suggestion `f(&x)`. The two sub-requirements are therefore jointly unsatisfiable in Rust, and the measured fragment substitutes the borrow marker `&` at the argument position, which is the standard mechanism that preserves the most of the task: (1) and (3) intact, (2) weakened. Under the deterministic tie-break ('some but not all' -> PARTIAL), support is PARTIAL with P-letter a. NOTE FOR THE AUDITOR, because it cuts against Rust downstream and must not be read as a reward: this forced `&` is exactly what makes Rust's determinacy at this probe B = 1, the lowest value the axis admits, and what keeps H2 from triggering. The coverage cost (1.0 of 2 points) and the metric-B benefit both follow from the same language rule, and doc 01's `determinacy_is_not_a_support_criterion` clause makes them separate channels by design. R10 form selection among forms that deliver (1) and (3): `f(&x);` = 23 tokens total (selected); `f(&x[..]);` = 26; `f(x.clone());` = 26 and is additionally rejected by the task's explicit ban on a clone at the argument position. F-2/F-3/F-4/F-6 are all satisfied: language and bundled std only, builds and runs under the frozen recipe with exit 0 and no warnings, no extra flag, no normative prohibition. HARNESS DISCLOSURE (spec 10.4): rustc rejects '.' in a crate name, so the frozen file F<nn>.P<k>.rs is copied byte-for-byte to F<nn>_P<k>.rs and the frozen command is run on the copy, with no added flag. AUDIT DISCLOSURE (F05.P1 comparability): this probe's canonical_task requires the plainest ordinary call 'with NO extra sigil, address-of, borrow marker, copy, clone, wrapper, annotation, or modifier at the argument position', and the frozen Rust fragment is `f(&x)`. Rust is the only one of the ten with a sigil at the argument position. B = 1 and the non-trigger of H2 are direct consequences of that `&` (the enumeration says so: '`&` is a local token marking an explicit borrow'), so those two figures are NOT answers to the same question the other nine answered and must be read as NOT-COMPARABLE at this probe rather than on the common basis. The honest Rust outcome the probe is built to expose is that the plainest parameter form `fn f(v: Vec<i32>)` with the bare call `f(x)` makes sub-requirement (3) fail to compile with E0382 (borrow of moved value) -- verified in this audit. The PARTIAL support and 1.0/2 capability points already record the deviation; the B and H figures now carry it too. [CROSS-LANGUAGE CONSISTENCY AUDIT 2026-09-18]

hidden_items.why: Local site 1, `let x = vec![1, 2, 3];`. The heap buffer this statement obtains is released when `x` is dropped at scope exit, with no `defer`, `drop` or `close` token written anywhere - the mandated LED illustration in section 1.2.1 ('a scope exit that runs a user-visible destructor ... with no locally written token naming it -> H4 triggers'). The ALLOCATION is NOT counted: `vec![...]` is a container literal, which is H4's first exclusion. NOT counted at local site 2: H2 does not trigger at `f(&x);`, which is the contrast this probe exists to draw. The mandated illustration for H2 is 'a call f(x) ... where f may be declared to take its parameter by writable reference ... with nothing at the call site distinguishing this from a by-value call'. Rust's call site is not in that position: `&` is a local token marking an explicit borrow (H2's fourth exclusion) and Reference 'Shared references' makes the aliasing read-only (H2's second exclusion), and both readings are refuted on the record by REFUT_M2_mutate (E0596). H3 does not trigger: Rust has no function overloading, so the path `f` resolves to exactly one item and the candidate set has cardinality 1. H5 does not trigger: over the probe's declared input domain the frozen `f` body is `v[0]` on a three-element vector and cannot panic, so condition 1 (occurrence) fails; allocation failure is excluded by the universal resource-exhaustion exclusion of section 0.8. H9 does not trigger for the same reason - the frozen `f` touches no state outside the fragment.

Local site 2, `f(&x);`. Control may leave this site abnormally -- any conforming completion of `f` may panic and unwind out of `probe` -- and no token at the site marks that possibility. AUDIT CORRECTION, and the reason the pre-audit zero was wrong: two readings of methodology 04 section 1.3.0 condition 1 ('when the probe's frozen implementation is executed over the probe's declared input domain') were in use across the corpus. Python, C++, Go, Java, Kotlin, TypeScript and Zig adjudicate over ANY conforming completion of `f` ('the domain places no constraint on `f`'s body') and charge H5; Rust and Quidra adjudicated over the frozen `f` body only and charged nothing. The confound that made the frozen-body reading look tenable is that the callee was not held constant: cpp, go, typescript, kotlin and java were frozen with a MUTATING `f` (their probes print 99) while quidra, swift and rust were frozen with an inert one (theirs print 1). determinacy_enumeration: V1 - the source is a heap-backed owning sequence. `xs.into_iter()` moves the source's buffer into the iterator (A8 = move, source invalidated), `map` is lazy and allocates nothing, `collect` produces a `Vec<i32>`, and the source buffer's fate is decided inside the statement. Witness: witnesses/F05.P3/rust/V1_heap_source/f05p3_vec2.rs, fragment byte-identical, completes the program with `let xs: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];` and installs a counting `#[global_allocator]`; it builds under the frozen recipe and prints `result=-1 allocs=0 deallocs=0` - the in-place-collect path reuses the moved source buffer, so the span performs NO allocation at all.

V2 - the source is an inline, non-heap iterable whose `into_iter` yields `i32` by value. There is no buffer to move (A8 = no observable resource event for the source) and `collect` must therefore obtain a fresh one (A8 = allocation occurs). Witness: witnesses/F05.P3/rust/V2_inline_source/f05p3_opt.rs, fragment byte-identical, completes the program with `let xs: Option<i32> = Some(1);` and the same counting allocator; it builds under the frozen recipe and prints `result=-1 allocs=1 deallocs=0`. The two witnesses differ in materiality dimension 6 through a channel Rule 1.2.2 names explicitly - a replaceable global allocator - so the difference is material and is not a performance artefact. EXCLUDED CLASSES with citations and refutations: a source whose `into_iter` yields REFERENCES rather than values is not realizable, because `neg` takes `i32` by value - refutation: completing the program with `let xs: [i32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];` is rejected under the frozen recipe's default edition with `error[E0631]: type mismatch in closure arguments ... note: expected closure signature `fn(&_) -> _`, found closure signature `fn(_) -> _``, since in editions before 2021 `array.into_iter()` resolves to the slice iterator; A8 = 'copy/clone may run user code' is excluded because the element type is fixed to `i32` by `neg`'s written parameter type and `i32` is `Copy`; A9 = 'may suspend/resume later' is excluded because Rust has no implicit suspension and no `await` is written (Reference, 'Await expressions'); A4 alternatives for the result are excluded by the written `Vec<i32>` annotation; Rule 1.4.8 token substitution is LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE.

V3 - the source sequence is EMPTY. `xs` is given context OUTSIDE the measured fragment, and methodology 03 Rule 1.1.2 states in terms that everything outside the fragment -- 'explicitly including declarations the probe designates as given context' -- is external, so the empty case is realizable with the 39 measured tokens byte-identical. `collect` then yields an empty `Vec<i32>` and `ys[0]` PANICS and unwinds instead of producing a value: A6 = may trap/panic/abort, A9 = may unwind / may not return, and the observable result (dimension 9) differs. WITNESS, built and run in this audit: scratchpad/rustaudit/f05p3_empty.rs, fragment byte-identical, `rustc -O -C debug-assertions=on`, terminates with 'index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0', exit 101. AUDIT CORRECTION: go (V2), java (V2), swift (V3) and typescript (K2) each enumerate this class with a built-and-run witness while cpp, python, rust, kotlin and zig did not; the justifications offered for the omission appealed to the 'declared input domain', which is a methodology 04 concept (it appears only in 04, at H1/H5/H8 and section 1.4.0) and does not govern Determinacy, which 03 Rule 1.1.2 governs. [CROSS-LANGUAGE CONSISTENCY AUDIT 2026-09-18]

V4 - `k` is a value of a user type with a user `Sub` implementation, so the `-` written inside the closure is a USER-REDEFINABLE OPERATOR. `k` is given context outside the fragment (Rule 1.1.2); `let ys: Vec<i32>` pins only the closure's Output type, not the left operand's type, so `impl Sub<i32> for K { type Output = i32; }` with a body that prints, allocates or panics is realizable with the fragment byte-identical. Rule 1.4.7 mandates this class in terms: 'A user-redefinable operator DOES add branches, because it makes classes reachable (allocation, failure, mutation, arbitrary control flow) that the built-in operator cannot reach.' A8 = allocation may occur, A9 = may unwind / may not return, A2 = state outside the fragment may be written. WITNESS, built and run in this audit: scratchpad/rustaudit/f05p3_userop.rs (`struct K` with `impl Sub<i32> for K` whose body prints, allocates a `Vec`, and panics), fragment byte-identical, `rustc -O -C debug-assertions=on` builds clean, the program prints 'user Sub ran, allocating' and then terminates with 'user operator panicked', exit 101. AUDIT CORRECTION: cpp counts exactly this class (T-user-operator, B3 witness), swift counts it (V2) and python counts it (user `__sub__`/`__rsub__`); the pre-audit Rust record's excluded_classes did not mention operator overloading at all, so this was an omission rather than an adjudicated exclusion with the Rule 1.3.1.e citation and refutation witness the schema requires. hidden_items.why: Local site 1, `let neg = |a: i32| k - a;`. Sub-test H8a fires at the subtraction inside the closure body, which section 0.7 makes local to this top-level statement: for the same operand type `i32`, Rust Reference 'Overflow' gives a panic when overflow checks are enabled and two's-complement wraparound when they are not, and the source says nothing about which build produced the binary. This is the mandated LED illustration of section 1.2.1 for a build-mode-dependent arithmetic edge. No local token selects the behaviour - Rust has `wrapping_sub`/`checked_sub`/`saturating_sub`, and the canonical task's `k - a` does not use one. The item counts once. NOT counted at this site: H2, because the capture of `k` is by shared reference and cannot write it; H4, because constructing a closure allocates nothing.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H3 - Overload or dynamic dispatch not locally evident
hidden_items.why: Local site 2, `let ys: Vec<i32> = xs.into_iter().map(neg).collect();`. `into_iter` is a trait method whose receiver `xs` is declared elsewhere and is therefore not local to this site (section 0.7); `core::iter::IntoIterator` is open to user implementations, so the set of candidate bodies compatible with the local site has cardinality >= 2, and they are not observationally equivalent - determinacy branches V1 and V2 are two built and run programs whose allocation behaviour at this very span differs (0 versus 1). The candidate-equivalence exclusion is universal in scope (section 1.4.0) and cannot be discharged for an open trait. Counted once for the statement: `map`, `collect` and `ys[0]` add no second event, because `Iterator::map` and `FromIterator for Vec<i32>` each have one body once the target type is pinned by the written annotation, and `ys`'s type is written at the site.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: Local site 2, same statement. Two implicit resource events occur here with no local token, and they are one event under section 1.3.2 because they arise from the same drop rule at the same local site: the `vec::IntoIter` temporary that `into_iter` produces is created and destroyed inside the statement, releasing or handing on the source buffer, and `ys` itself is dropped at scope exit, freeing the result buffer - neither is named by a `defer`, `drop`, `close` or `using` token. Mandated LED illustration, section 1.2.1 (scope exit running a destructor with nothing written for it). The ALLOCATION at `collect` is NOT counted: `collect` is a factory call whose documented meaning is building a new collection, which is H4's first exclusion; V1's measured `allocs=0` additionally shows that no allocation need occur there at all. H5 does NOT trigger: `ys[0]` panics only on an out-of-range index, and over the probe's declared input domain `ys` has three elements; allocation failure is excluded by section 0.8.

complexity_detail.description: Closure capture-mode inference: a non-`move` closure captures each used place by the least demanding mode - shared borrow, then unique borrow, then move - decided by how the body uses it.
Which of `Fn`, `FnMut` and `FnOnce` a closure implements is decided by how it uses its captures, not by anything written in the closure expression.
Every closure expression has a unique anonymous type; two closures with identical signatures are different types and cannot be used interchangeably without a coercion or a trait object.
The target type of `collect` is chosen by inference from the annotation or turbofish, not written at the call; without one the call is ambiguous.
complexity_detail.citation: Rust Reference, 'Type inference'; std `Iterator::collect`; rustc E0282

complexity_detail.description: Integer overflow is a program error whose outcome is fixed by whether overflow checks are enabled, with nothing written at the operation.
Values are dropped at the end of their scope, and temporaries at the end of the enclosing statement.
Standard-library clause: `IntoIterator::into_iter` takes the collection by value; `impl IntoIterator for Vec<T>` consumes the vector and yields `T` by value.
Standard-library clause: `Iterator::map` is lazy - it returns an adaptor and calls the closure only as the adaptor is advanced.
Standard-library clause: `Iterator::collect` consumes the iterator, driving it to completion, and builds a collection through `FromIterator`.
Standard-library clause: `impl<T> FromIterator<T> for Vec<T>` builds a new `Vec` owning a heap buffer.
Standard-library clause: indexing a `Vec<T>` with a `usize` returns the element and panics if out of bounds.
